en: When guard cells absorb water, they swell and open the stomata to allow carbon dioxide into the leaf for photosynthesis.
A camel's hump stores fat that the body breaks down to release energy and produce metabolic water when desert food and drinking water are scarce.
Oxygen from inhaled air passes through the thin walls of alveoli into the blood, while carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the lungs to be exhaled.
The stomach secretes hydrochloric acid to break down food and kill harmful bacteria before the partially digested mixture moves into the small intestine.
A frog tadpole breathes underwater using gills, but as it metamorphoses into an adult, it develops lungs to breathe air on land.
Fungi and bacteria break down dead organisms, returning essential nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus to the soil for plants to absorb and reuse.
Water evaporates from the leaves through transpiration, creating a pulling force that draws more water and dissolved minerals up the xylem from the roots.
When you touch a hot object, sensory nerves send a signal to the spinal cord, which instantly triggers motor nerves to pull your hand away.
Macrophages, a type of white blood cell, engulf and digest invading bacteria, triggering an immune response to protect the body from infection.
A bat emits high-pitched sound waves that bounce off flying insects, allowing the bat to determine the prey's exact location using the returning echoes.
As bees collect nectar, pollen sticks to their fuzzy bodies and transfers to the stigma of the next flower, enabling plant fertilization and seed production.
When the brain sends an electrical signal, muscle fibers slide past each other and shorten, pulling on attached tendons to bend the bone at the joint.
